summary: This experimental RFC specifies receiver-driven Low Extra Delay Background Transport, mechanisms letting the receiver run a less-than-best-effort congestion control algorithm for TCP. It is a product of the ICCRG of the IRTF.

plainLanguage.summary: Some downloads can wait in the back seat. Here the receiving side slows a background download so urgent traffic goes first.

questions: how does rledbat control the tcp sender
what is less than best effort traffic
how does a tcp receiver detect retransmissions
subtitle: Lets a TCP receiver slow a background download by shrinking the window it advertises, with no change to the sender.

tldr.problem: LEDBAT and LEDBAT++ are less-than-best-effort congestion controls run by the sender, so a receiver cannot ask for background treatment when the sender, a CDN or a proxy does not cooperate.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver measures delay and loss from TCP timestamps and sequence numbers, runs an LBE algorithm, and advertises the result in the TCP receive window. A standard TCP sender then sends at the smaller of its own window and that one.
tldr.outcome: The flow can never be more aggressive than standard TCP, and the document is an Experimental RFC from the IRTF that invites more experiments.

facts.label: Window Scale
facts.value: Client SHOULD use values lower than 12

facts.label: Sender changes needed
facts.value: None; sender must support RFC 9293 and Timestamps

today: RFC 9840 is an Experimental RFC from the IRTF's Internet Congestion Control Research Group, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. The text says rLEDBAT is available in several operating systems and has been deployed by Microsoft in services such as Windows update.

sections.title: Why a Receiver-Driven Approach
sections.content:
LEDBAT is a congestion control algorithm for less-than-best-effort (LBE) traffic. It backs off earlier than standard TCP so that other traffic gets the capacity, and it aims to keep queuing delay near a target. LEDBAT and LEDBAT++ are run at the sender. rLEDBAT is a set of mechanisms that lets the receiver of a TCP connection run such an algorithm instead.

The RFC names three motivations. With a CDN that does not support LBE, the content owner cannot get background behavior even when it controls the client. Proxies and middleboxes terminate TCP connections, which blocks end-to-end LBE. And a mobile device cannot manage its downlink with sender-based algorithms, but with rLEDBAT it can treat some incoming traffic as background.
sections.plainLanguage: Usually only the sender can decide to go slowly. rLEDBAT lets the person receiving ask for slow, polite delivery, which helps when the sender or the middle of the path will not cooperate.

sections.title: Steering the Sender with the Receive Window
sections.content:
The rLEDBAT receiver controls the sender's rate through the TCP receive window. The sender must implement RFC 9293 and the TCP Timestamps option, and needs no rLEDBAT-specific changes. The receiver MUST use an LBE congestion control algorithm and SHOULD use LEDBAT or LEDBAT++. The algorithm itself is out of scope.

The receiver MUST NOT advertise more than the normal flow control value fcwnd, and SHOULD advertise the minimum of RLWND (the rLEDBAT window) and fcwnd. The sender's window is SND.WND = min(cwnd, RLWND, fcwnd), so an rLEDBAT flow is never more aggressive than standard TCP. At the start of a connection RLWND is at its maximum.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender already follows two limits: how much it thinks the network can take and how much the receiver says it can take. rLEDBAT just makes the receiver's number smaller when it wants to go gently.

sections.title: Window Changes Without Shrinking
sections.content:
Cutting the advertised window below what is already in flight is called shrinking the window, and RFC 9293 discourages it. So the receiver SHOULD NOT shrink the window. It MUST only reduce RCV.WND by the number of bytes in a received data packet and keep reducing step by step until the target is reached. This may take up to one RTT, which is enough because LEDBAT and LEDBAT++ do at most one multiplicative decrease per RTT.

The Window Scale option limits how finely the window can be announced. Values 0 to 11 have no impact for rLEDBAT with an MSS of around 1500 bytes, while larger values make control coarse. For example, at 14 one window unit is 10 MSS. The client SHOULD therefore set Window Scale values lower than 12.
sections.plainLanguage: You may not snatch back water already poured. So the receiver closes the tap a little with every cup that arrives, until it reaches the level it wants.

sections.title: Measuring Delay and Detecting Loss
sections.content:
To estimate queuing delay, LEDBAT++ subtracts the base RTT from the current RTT, while LEDBAT uses one-way delay. The receiver MUST enable the TCP Timestamps option and matches the TSval it sends with the TSecr it gets back, which works even for a pure receiver. When several packets share a TSval, RTT is taken from the first packet with that value. Delayed ACKs can add up to 500 ms to some samples, so the receiver can discard such samples or use a MIN filter.

For one-way delay, the receiver subtracts the packet's timestamp from the local arrival time. It must learn the timestamp units and clock skew. A mismatch of 100 ppm gives 6 ms of variation per minute. The receiver may force periodic slowdowns to measure these.

Retransmissions are detected when a new segment has SEG.SEQ lower than RCV.HGH but TSV.SEQ higher than TSV.HGH. This fails for window tail drops, in which case the sender's own congestion control reacts.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver times how long messages take and watches for repeats of things it already saw out of order. Longer times or repeats mean the road is crowded, so it asks for slower delivery.

sections.title: Security and Experiment Considerations
sections.content:
The authors believe rLEDBAT adds no new vulnerabilities to TCP endpoints, since it uses the receive window and timestamps. An attacker could fake delay by delaying packets or editing timestamps, but would need to be on path, where simply reducing RCV.WND is more direct. An attacker could also fake a loss by injecting a packet with the correct sequence number, ports and addresses, which may slightly expand the attack surface.

The experiment asks how the sender's and receiver's congestion controls interact, including CUBIC, BBR and LEDBAT(++), how rLEDBAT interacts with active queue management such as CoDel, PIE and L4S, and how it should resume after idle periods. The text lists implementations in Windows 11, Windows Server 2022, macOS and iOS, Linux and ns-3.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor who can already mess with the traffic could slow you down anyway. The new trick lets someone also fake a repeat packet, but not much more.

items.title: Delay measurement
items.text: RTT or one-way delay from TCP timestamps, used to estimate queuing delay.

items.title: Loss detection
items.text: A segment with a lower sequence number but a later timestamp is a retransmission.

items.title: Receive window control
items.text: Turns the LBE congestion window into an advertised RCV.WND without shrinking it.
